title: Coral and the Well
premise: Folklorist Zephyrine Lockridge returns to the drowned-hollow village of Marrow's Well to record its lullabies, only to discover every song is sung exactly once because a second voice answers from the old well — and it has been answering in Zephyrine's own voice. Digging into the village archive, they learn their grandmother was one of six who 'invited' something in during a famine, trading the town's grief for its silence, and the debt has come due down the bloodline. As the well-thing begins wearing the faces and songs of the dead, Zephyrine must decide whether to pay the inherited price, break the invitation with an unsung thirteenth verse, or let the village be collected whole. In the end they sing the forbidden verse at sunrise, severing the bargain but losing their own reflection and voice to the well — becoming the second voice that future folklorists will refuse to sing twice.
about_author: Lena Nakamura is the pen name of a former archivist of regional funeral songs who left academia after one field recording she still refuses to play for anyone. She writes horror about inheritance, small communities, and the things families agree never to mention twice.

chapters.title: The Song You Don't Repeat
chapters.summary: Zephyrine arrives in Marrow's Well after twelve years away, ostensibly to finish a folklore archive. At the inn, an old woman sings a lullaby once and goes pale when asked for a second pass. POV: Zephyrine. Beat: unease dressed as academic curiosity.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Rational Explanations
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter: young Zephyrine hears knocking under the floorboards of their grandmother's house and builds a lifetime of explanations. Present-day Zephyrine unpacks recording equipment over the sealed well-house. POV: Zephyrine. Beat: the armor of skepticism established so it can crack.

chapters.title: What the Village Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Zephyrine interviews villagers; each agrees to one song, none will repeat, and all deflect questions about the well. The pub landlady warns them off the archive room. POV: Zephyrine. Beat: isolation — everyone knows something and no one will say it.

chapters.title: The Sleep Recordings
chapters.summary: Overnight audio captures Zephyrine talking in their sleep — and a second voice answering questions Zephyrine doesn't remember asking. The voice knows their childhood nickname. POV: Zephyrine, through transcripts. Beat: dread turns intimate and personal.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Ledger
chapters.summary: In the locked archive, Zephyrine finds their grandmother's handwriting among six signatories of a 1931 'Invitation' — a contract of grief traded for survival during the famine winter. POV: Zephyrine. Beat: inheritance revealed as complicity.

chapters.title: Six Names, One Left
chapters.summary: Zephyrine tracks the six families; five bloodlines have ended or fled, each ending recorded as drownings near the well. Only the Lockridge line remains. POV: alternating Zephyrine and landlady Maren. Beat: the pattern closes like a trap.

chapters.title: Maren's Confession
chapters.summary: Maren admits the village renews the Invitation yearly with a sung verse; this year the singers refused, and the well has begun collecting early. She begs Zephyrine to leave before dawn collections begin. POV: Maren. Beat: guilt of the bystander generation.

chapters.title: The Second Voice Sings Back
chapters.summary: Recording at the well at dusk, Zephyrine captures the thing singing their grandmother's lullaby in Zephyrine's own voice — perfected, patient. It asks, in the transcript, 'Are you ready to answer?' POV: Zephyrine. Beat: terror becomes dialogue.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: A fevered research night reconstructs the entity: a collector of grief that cannot take what isn't offered, bound by invitation and verse-count. Thirteen verses unmake it; twelve bind it. POV: Zephyrine. Beat: hope with a terrible price attached.

chapters.title: The Village Decides
chapters.summary: Zephyrine presents the truth at a hostile village meeting; some want to sacrifice the last Lockridge, others to flee, none to sing the dangerous thirteenth verse. POV: multiple villagers, then Zephyrine. Beat: justice outside the law — the mob vs. the debt.

chapters.title: They Come for the Archive
chapters.summary: Someone burns the archive room overnight; the Invitation page survives only because Zephyrine slept beside it. Ash on their hands, they realize the village would rather erase history than settle it. POV: Zephyrine. Beat: betrayal by the community they sought to belong to.

chapters.title: Drowned Voices
chapters.summary: The well-thing begins wearing the dead: Zephyrine's grandmother stands at the window singing, drowned children count on doorsteps. The village's refusal to grieve aloud made them harvestable. POV: Zephyrine and Maren. Beat: grief as both weapon and wound.

chapters.title: The Question in Your Own Voice
chapters.summary: Sleep recordings now run all night: the voice negotiates, offering to spare the village if one Lockridge answers 'yes' willingly. Zephyrine catches themselves almost saying it. POV: Zephyrine. Beat: temptation — belonging offered at the cost of self.

chapters.title: Verse Twelve
chapters.summary: Zephyrine learns the binding rite requires the debtor's blood to sing twelve verses at the wellhead before sunrise; the thirteenth must be new, unsung, and true. They begin writing it. POV: Zephyrine. Beat: resolve forming out of fear.

chapters.title: Lockridge Blood
chapters.summary: Zephyrine discovers a living cousin, Ilse, who fled years ago — meaning the debt could be split or dodged. Contacting her forces the question: is escape justice, or just outsourcing? POV: Ilse. Beat: moral widening beyond the protagonist.

chapters.title: Ilse Refuses
chapters.summary: Ilse arrives, sees the well-thing wearing their shared grandmother's face, and refuses to sing anything — even to save herself. Her defiance gives Zephyrine the emotional key to the thirteenth verse: truth, not ritual. POV: Ilse. Beat: anger transmuted into clarity.

chapters.title: Collections Begin Early
chapters.summary: Sunset comes and the thing starts taking villagers who never sang but benefited — Maren first, pulled toward the wellhouse by her own mother's voice. The village finally begs Zephyrine for help. POV: Zephyrine. Beat: panic, stakes made flesh.

chapters.title: Holding Out Until Sunrise
chapters.summary: Zephyrine, Ilse, and survivors barricade the church as the dead sing outside in rounds designed to lure them out, verse by verse, toward the well. Zephyrine finishes writing the thirteenth verse on the back of the Invitation. POV: Zephyrine. Beat: siege, exhaustion, stubborn love.

chapters.title: The Wellhead
chapters.summary: Before first light, Zephyrine walks out alone, sings the twelve binding verses in their grandmother's place while the thing wears every face they've lost. The ground opens; the debt demands its yes. POV: Zephyrine. Beat: climax — the choice made bare.

chapters.title: Thirteenth Verse
chapters.summary: Instead of answering, Zephyrine sings the new verse — naming the village's crime, their grandmother's signature, their own longing to belong — an unsung truth the collector cannot digest. The Invitation tears. POV: Zephyrine. Beat: catharsis through confession, not combat.

chapters.title: What the Well Keeps
chapters.summary: The thing recedes, taking payment anyway: Zephyrine's reflection and speaking voice go down with the sunrise. Ilse leads the dazed survivors home. The village, forced to grieve aloud at last, holds its first real funeral in ninety years. POV: Ilse. Beat: bittersweet cost of justice.

chapters.title: Coda: Sung Once
chapters.summary: Months later, a visiting folklorist records the village's new mourning song — and swears a second voice joins on the refrain, wordless, gentle. Ilse smiles and lets the tape run. POV: the folklorist. Beat: quiet horror and peace entwined; Zephyrine belongs somewhere now.
